# Kilesa Saṁyutta (SN 27)

**ID:** SN 27
**Section:** Saṁyuttanikāya (sn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Kilesa Saṁyutta
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0303m.mul5.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Kilesasaṁyutta* (SN 27), titled "Linked Discourses on Corruptions" or "Connected Discourses on Defilements", is the twenty-seventh saṁyutta of the *Saṁyuttanikāya* [Bodhi 2003; Bodhi 2003_x]. It forms the third collection in a sequence of three closely related saṁyuttas—alongside the *Okkantisaṁyutta* (SN 25) and the *Uppādasaṁyutta* (SN 26)—that are built upon an identical tenfold scheme classifying the factors of experience: the six internal sense bases, six external sense bases, six classes each of consciousness, contact, feeling, perception, volition, and craving (such as the *Taṇhā Sutta*, SN 27.8), as well as the six elements and five aggregates [Bodhi 2003_x; Le 2018; Willemen et al. 1998]. Across these ten items, the text teaches that desire and lust (*chanda-rāga*) directed toward any of these phenomena constitutes a corruption or defilement of the mind (*cittass' eso upakkileso*) [Bodhi 2003; Hazra 1994; Le 2018]. When a monastic abandons this mental corruption, the mind inclines toward renunciation (*nekkhamma*) and becomes malleable and wieldy for direct knowledge [Bodhi 2003; Le 2018]. Buddhaghosa's commentary (*Sāratthappakāsinī*) observes that although the chapter title uses *kilesa*, the discourses use *upakkilesa*, explaining that it corrupts the supramundane mind by obstructing its arising [Bodhi 2003_x].

 Text-reuse computations by DharmaNexus align SN 27 with 569 matching passages across 25 Pali canonical and post-canonical works, most significantly with its companion collection, the *Uppāda Saṁyutta* (SN 26; 119 matches), the *Aṅguttaranikāya* (AN 6 and AN 11), the *Khandha Saṁyutta* (SN 22), the *Bojjhaṅga Saṁyutta* (SN 46), and the *Rāhula Saṁyutta* (SN 18) [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also detects shared formulaic phrasing in Sanskrit and Tibetan versions of the *Śatasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā* and *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā* [DharmaNexus]. Modern scholars have noted that the tenfold categories structured within the *Okkanti-*, *Uppāda-*, and *Kilesasaṁyutta* served as early scriptural precedents for the subsequent Abhidharma categorization of mental factors into tenfold classifications [Willemen et al. 1998].
